newsitem.title: DUBAI: British nurses in Saudi murder case get legal help.
newsitem.headline: British nurses in Saudi murder case get legal help.

text.p: A Saudi Arabian law firm said on Tuesday it would provide legal advice for two British nurses charged with the murder of an Australian colleague and stressed Islamic sharia law would ensure them a fair trial.

"We have...accepted, at their request, to provide legal advice and support to the two English nurses who have been accused in a murder case of an Australian nurse at King Fahd Hospital in the eastern province," said the law firm of Salah al-Hejailan in a statement in answer to questions by Reuters.
The firm said it has not yet studied the files of the case or met Deborah Kim Parry, 41, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, who have been charged with murdering Yvonne Gilford, 55.
They were arrested on December 20, nine days after Gilford was found stabbed and beaten to death, and are being held at a prison in the Saudi eastern town of Dammam.
If found guilty the two could be publicly executed by the sword. However, Saudi ambassador to London Ghazi Alghosaibi said that "the death sentence is not automatic".
Diplomats said the British embassy and the law firm were seeking access for the legal advisers to see the two this week.
A British Foreign Office spokesman in London said on Monday consul Tim Lamb met the two nurses on Monday separately for 15 minutes each.
"Both women seemed in good health but were obviously concerned about the charges levelled against them," he said.

The Hejailan law firm said in its statement that the killing of the Australian nurse "has touched upon the feelings of the Saudi community as the offence has been allegedly committed by foreigners who are members of the nursing profession which is generally believed to be a profession of mercy".

It said suspects had "the right...to have a fair trial. This involves magisterial inquiry to be conducted by a judge, the right of the accused to seek legal assistance and to be assisted by a translator..."

Western media reports and human rights groups had criticised the Saudi legal system, saying suspects had no right to defence lawyers pleading for them in court as in the West and foreigners were not provided with translators.

The law firm said a defence lawyer would speak on behalf of the nurses in court and could conduct a form of cross examination. There would be no prosecution lawyer, only a police report with the judge handling the rest of prosecution case.

Hejailan's law firm said under sharia the victim's family could ask for blood money which would spare the suspects the death penalty. The family could also waive the right to ask for blood money, in which case the court would "decide on the right of the state. Punishment in respect of such right is usually a sentence of imprisonment for five years".
It said the head of state can however cancel the sentence.
Under sharia a victim's family, regardless of religion or nationality, can ask for the death sentence be dropped in return for a financial settlement, referred to as blood money.
